opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so Dobby is my little house elf. I'd been running a pile of separate apps for the lights, the shades, the HVAC, the pool, the security cameras, the Sonos, and every one had its own janky interface. At some point I thought: why am I tapping through six apps when I can just talk to an agent?

So I pointed an LLM agent at my local network. It scanned around, found all the devices, figured out the APIs, some of them undocumented, and wrote the glue code itself. Now I just text Dobby over WhatsApp: "Dobby, sleepy time," and the lights go down, the shades close, the thermostat adjusts. It also watches the cameras, so if someone pulls into the driveway it sends me a picture and a little description of who's there.

What I find compelling is less the home automation and more what it says about software in general. All those apps were, in a sense, built for a person to click through. But there's a different consumer now. The agent doesn't need a beautiful UI, it needs an API it can call. So the whole thing collapses: the apps kind of disappear and you're left with one natural-language interface over everything.

I think that's a preview of where a lot of software is heading. Much of it is just going to be exposed as endpoints for agents, and the human-facing layer becomes a conversation. Also, honestly, it was just fun. I vibe-coded the whole thing in an afternoon or two, which would have been a multi-week project a few years ago. That delta is the part I keep coming back to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he used to run separate apps for household devices and now talks to Dobby as one natural-language interface over them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Dobby is basically the name I gave to the little agent that runs the house. And honestly the thing I find compelling is less about the home automation itself and more about what it tells you about where the interface is going.

For a long time, controlling your home meant going through some app with a bunch of menus. You open the app, you find the room, you find the device, you tap the slider. It's fine, but it's a lot of ceremony for "I'm cold." With Dobby I just say, "it's a bit cold in here," and it figures out that that probably means nudge the thermostat up a degree or two, not blast the heat. That translation from a fuzzy human intent into a specific action is the thing the LLM is really good at, and it turns out it's what you actually want from an interface most of the time.

The other piece I like is composition. The individual devices all have these narrow APIs: lights on, lights off, set brightness. But the interesting requests are compound. "I'm going to bed" is really six or seven things: lock the door, turn off the downstairs lights, dim the bedroom, lower the thermostat, maybe check if the garage is closed. I never wrote a "bedtime routine." Dobby just knows what going to bed implies and chains the tools together. And if I say "actually leave the hallway light on," it just adapts. You'd never ship that level of flexibility in a hardcoded automation.

And then there's the slightly deeper thing, which is that it's a nice sandbox for agents in general. The home is a bounded world. There's a fixed set of tools, the stakes are low, and I can watch it make mistakes in a very legible way. When it does something dumb, like turning on all the lights because I was ambiguous, I learn something about how the model interprets instructions and how I should expose the tools to it. It's a lot of the same questions you'd have about agents doing software or operating a browser, just in a setting where the worst case is the lights are wrong for ten seconds.

So I'd say the compelling part is that it's a really concrete, daily, non-hypothetical version of "the computer understands what I mean." I don't have to think about the system. I just talk to it like I'd talk to a person who happens to live in the walls.

r001.rationale: The response presents Dobby as replacing menu-based app control, but it does not identify multiple separate home-automation apps as what it replaces.

astra-6.text:
What’s compelling to me is the idea that you can describe the outcome you want instead of figuring out which app or setting controls it. You say, “I’m going to bed,” and the system can translate that into actions across the house. The interface is your intent.

But the interesting challenge is making that reliable. Does it understand what you meant? Does it know when to ask a question? Can you undo what it did? A home is a very concrete place to explore those questions, because the software is actually changing the environment around you.

r001.rationale: It says you can state the outcome you want instead of figuring out which app or setting controls it, and the system can act across the house.

sol-6.1.text: What I find compelling is that your home has all these capabilities, but they’re scattered across apps and interfaces. With natural language, you can express what you actually want—“I’m going to bed”—instead of specifying every individual action. The system can translate that intent into turning off lights, adjusting the temperature, whatever you’ve configured. But the interesting challenge is making that reliable and predictable. If it’s controlling your physical environment, you want to understand what it’s going to do and have a very easy way to correct it.

r001.rationale: It says home capabilities are scattered across apps and interfaces, then presents natural-language commands as a way to express intent instead of specifying each action.
